change: adopted: pooled revision (ii) cap+A2, configuration A, Madison on the Madison-like path; lower = mean of Rhode Island and Oregon; Milwaukee at its measured 2022-2025 rate
description: The three scenarios as adopted.

change: Lower as a statistical 10th percentile of the between-state spread (the Gate 3 lower: central levels / 1.804)
description: The lower scenario is set at the 10th percentile of how much the eight statewide-law states' levels differ (every place's central level divided by 1.804), as at Gate 3, instead of the average of the two slowest states, Rhode Island and Oregon. That level is below every statewide-law state's. Only the lower changes.

change: Madison at its pooled level (no Madison-like path)
description: Madison follows the statewide estimate for places like it instead of the path that similar cities in Washington and Oregon took. This changes Madison's addition only, and through it the statewide total.

change: California out of the common level (configuration B)
description: The eight states' typical level is set without California. The central falls, and Strong adoption falls most, because California is the state that stretches the range upward. This alternative predicted the held-out states less well. The lower is the same Rhode Island and Oregon average, taken from this fit.

change: LA-calibrated multifamily correction (option iii, configuration A)
description: California's counts include ADUs on apartment and other multifamily properties, which the benchmark law does not allow. This removes more of them, using Los Angeles County parcel records. The lower is the same Rhode Island and Oregon average, taken from this fit.

change: no reporting-share correction (counts divided by every home in the state)
description: Maine, Massachusetts, Rhode Island 2025 and Utah report permits only for the towns that answered, but the rate divides them by every single-family home in the state. Here the counts are not scaled up for the towns that did not report (the Gate 4 treatment). Non-reporting towns are probably smaller and quieter, so the true figure is likely between this case and the adopted one. The lower is the Rhode Island and Oregon average from this fit.

change: reporting-share correction for Maine, Massachusetts and Rhode Island only (Utah not corrected)
description: Utah's share of homes in reporting places (about 80%) is computed here from the report lists; the other three use published town or population shares. This case leaves Utah uncorrected. The lower is the Rhode Island and Oregon average from this fit.

change: Washington's law years counted from enactment (July 2023), not local compliance
description: Washington's cities had to adopt compliant rules only from mid-2025. This case counts its law years from the 2023 enactment instead, as at Gate 4, so two years under old local rules count as law years. The lower is the Rhode Island and Oregon average from this fit.

change: Vermont 2024 dropped (57 ADUs from the state housing layer, counted by year built)
description: Vermont's 2024 count comes from the state's new-housing layer, not the regional planning commission's own series (which ends at 2023), and every Vermont count is by year built or first occupied, not permit year. Not adopted (AQ-062): it makes Vermont's own held-out miss worse. Refitted without that point, the 8-state reference line is 10,308 permits (adopted 10,308). The lower is the Rhode Island and Oregon average from this fit.

change: all three AQ-061 comparison-state changes undone (no coverage correction, Washington from enactment; Massachusetts still 11 months)
description: The comparison-state counts and coding as at Gate 4, on today's current-law rates. The lower is the Rhode Island and Oregon average from this fit.

change: every comparison year read against 2020-2024 homes (not year-matched)
description: Each comparison rate divides permits by single-family homes. The adopted fit matches homes to the year, from ACS 2020-2024 homes moved back or forward by one-unit building permits (AQ-064). Here every year uses 2020-2024 homes, as before AQ-064, so early years read a little low and 2025-2026 a little high. The lower is the Rhode Island and Oregon average from this fit.

change: Maine and Massachusetts reporting shares as homes shares (Maine 0.62, Massachusetts 0.809)
description: Maine's published share (0.73) counts people and Massachusetts' (0.835) counts towns. Reporting towns are mostly larger, so their share of single-family homes is likely lower: about 0.62 in Maine (the largest towns holding 73% of its people hold 62% of its detached homes) and 0.809 in Massachusetts (from a non-official copy of the state's tracker file, towns that answered only mid-year at half weight). The adopted fit keeps the published shares until official town lists are in hand. The lower is the Rhode Island and Oregon average from this fit.

change: Vermont dropped (left out of the comparison states)
description: Vermont is left out of the comparison states, because its counts are by year built or first occupied, not permit year. It is out of the typical level, the lower and upper spread and the reference line; seven states remain, California included. Not adopted (AQ-062): the other six states are predicted less well without it. The 8-state reference line becomes a 7-state line of 11,038 permits (adopted 10,308). The lower is the Rhode Island and Oregon average from this fit.

change: no top-code on the value gap (small high-value villages keep their extrapolated levels)
description: Eight areas (7 villages and towns, 2,852 homes) have home values further above Wisconsin's average than any California place is above California's. The adopted allocation top-codes their gap at California's largest (+1.01 in log terms). Without it they keep levels up to 7.6 per 1,000 homes per year. The statewide total barely moves; permits move between places.

change: no ramp (full rate from 2027; Madison's observed path unchanged)
description: In the adopted model the law reaches about 63%, 83% and 86% of its full effect in 2027, 2028 and 2029 (central), as it did in other states. Here it is at full strength from the first year.

change: rural and small-community places at the Madison floor (0.2345)
description: Rural areas and small communities, which have no measured activity, get only the minimum rate set from Madison's permits (0.2345 per 1,000 single-family homes per year) instead of their level from the statewide estimate. Shows how much of the addition comes from those places.

change: eligible-property basis without one-unit attached homes: permits per 1,000 properties eligible under each state's law (detached homes plus multifamily properties)
description: Rates are divided by the properties each state's law makes eligible (houses plus small multifamily properties) instead of by single-family homes. A separate model with its own baseline (636 permits); it was run at Gate 3 (Milwaukee on its assumed ramp) and is not rerun here, and its 10th-percentile lower is left out because the adopted lower is defined differently.

change: multiplicative: the law only multiplies each place's current rate by the pooled statewide-law factor
description: Each place's current rate is multiplied by one statewide factor, instead of rising to the level that similar places reached in the eight statewide-law states. Places that permit almost nothing today would stay near zero. Before-and-after counts in other states contradict this, but no Midwest state has data after a statewide law yet.
source: scripts/run_pooled_revision.py multiplicative(), refitted on the adopted current-law rates

change: California-only market regression (refitted on cap+A2 counts)
description: Wisconsin places are predicted from a model fitted on California cities alone, where cities like Madison responded weakly. A downside case.
source: scripts/run_pooled_revision.py ca_only_regression(), on the adopted current-law rates

change: Places with uncoded rules behave like prohibited places
description: Places whose ADU rules have not been coded (69% of single-family homes) behave like places that prohibit ADUs, instead of like places that restrict them. Changes only the current-law baseline; the law's addition moves the other way by about as much.
source: engine with only the current-law rate changed (reference/adu_model_baseline_only_effects.csv, case uncoded-prohibited)

change: No ramp for recently liberalized places (full current-law rate at once)
description: Places that loosened their ADU rules recently are at their new group's rate at once, instead of rising to it over a few years. Changes only the current-law baseline.
source: engine with only the current-law rate changed (reference/adu_model_baseline_only_effects.csv, case no-baseline-ramp)

change: Madison's current-law rate = its 2026 pace so far (provisional)
description: Madison's current-law rate is its 2026 pace so far (42 second homes, 1 January to 23 October, provisional) instead of its 2022-2025 rate. Changes only the current-law baseline; Madison's addition falls by about as much.
source: engine with only the current-law rate changed (reference/adu_model_baseline_only_effects.csv, case madison-2026)

change: Madison's current-law rate from 2024-2025 only
description: Madison's current-law rate uses 2024-2025 only. Changes only the current-law baseline.
source: engine with only the current-law rate changed (reference/adu_model_baseline_only_effects.csv, case madison-2024-2025)

change: Madison's current-law rate without the templated builder programme
description: Madison's 2022-2025 rate leaves out the one builder's programme of second homes. Changes only the current-law baseline.
source: engine with only the current-law rate changed (reference/adu_model_baseline_only_effects.csv, case madison-excl-templated)

change: Milwaukee rises to Madison's rate after its 2025 reform (assumed ramp)
description: Milwaukee rises from its pre-reform rate to Madison's rate within about four years of its August 2025 ADU reform (the assumed ramp used at Gate 3), instead of staying at its measured 2022-2025 rate. Changes only the current-law baseline; Milwaukee's addition falls by about as much.
source: engine with only the current-law rate changed (reference/adu_model_baseline_only_effects.csv, case milwaukee-ramp)

change: Wisconsin's baseline rises like no-law places (×1.11 a year)
description: Every Wisconsin place's current-law rate keeps rising as fast as in cities and states without a statewide ADU law: those rose about 1.5 times from their before-period to their after-period, four years later (about ×1.11 a year), almost entirely because of local reforms there. Wisconsin's main local reform (Madison 2021) is already in its measured rate, so this is a check rather than the main case. Changes only the current-law baseline; the law's addition falls by nearly as much.
source: engine with only the current-law rate changed (reference/adu_model_baseline_only_effects.csv, case wi-rising-like-nolaw)
